Patellar Maltracking and Instability/Dislocation
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Patellar maltracking and instability is a complex biomechanical problem after total knee
arthroplasty (TKA) in which the patella does not track centrally or anatomically within the
trochlear groove of the femoral implant.
A spectrum of severity of patellar maltracking exists, from mild lateral patellar tilt to frank
dislocation.
This displacement may result in anterior knee pain, reduced knee range of motion, quadriceps
weakness, and the sensation of knee instability.
Epidemiology
Patellofemoral instability or patella-related complications comprise 8% to 18% of revision
procedures after TKA.1,2
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Patellofemoral mechanics are dictated by several variables after TKA.
Patellar positioning on the femoral trochlea changes with the degree of knee flexion; foot
progression angle during the gait cycle; and forces exerted by soft tissues, predominately the
quadriceps muscles, which is dependent on the Q angle.3
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Patellofemoral maltracking usually results from a technical error at the time of TKA.
However, acute injuries after TKA also may lead to arthrotomy rupture and may lead to
patellar maltracking and/or instability.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The patellofemoral articulation is a complicated joint, with several degrees of movement
that are dynamic throughout knee range of motion. Patellar position on the femoral
trochlea changes with the degree of knee flexion; foot progression angle during the gait
cycle; and forces exerted by the surrounding soft tissues, predominately the quadriceps.
Many of these variables are dependent on a patient’s Q angle. Therefore, optimizing
patellofemoral knee mechanics after TKA is one of the most difficult aspects of the
procedure.3
Patellar maltracking and instability occur after TKA if the patella does not track centrally
within the trochlear groove of the femoral implant during knee range of motion. Revision
surgery after TKA for patellar-related complications encompasses 8% to 20% of all
revision TKA procedures.1,2 This displacement may cause anterior knee pain, either via
soft-tissue impingement or lateral facet remodeling or sclerosis, and frank dislocation.
This pain may then result in reduced knee range of motion, quadriceps inhibition and
weakness, and subjective knee instability. The etiology of patellar maltracking, outside of
an acute injury and arthrotomy dehiscence and/or extensor mechanism rupture, usually
is a technical error at the time of index TKA4,5 (Resources 1 and 2; Video 1).

Preoperative Risk Factors
Femoral or tibial malrotation
Femoral trochlear dysplasia
Previous patellofemoral realignment procedure
Preoperative valgus coronal alignment
Tight lateral soft-tissue envelope (valgus knee, severely stiff knee)
Component Risk Factors
Femoral component position: internal rotation, flexion, valgus, or medialization
Femoral component trochlear design: anatomic trochlear groove, thinner anterior flange
Tibial component position: internal rotation or medializations
Lateral patellar component placement

Risk Factors
With regard to risk factors, patellofemoral mechanics depend on a patient’s Q angle,
which is an angle subtended by the anterior superior iliac spine to the center of the
patella and from the center of the patella to the tibial tubercle.6 Component
malpositioning or malrotation results in changes in the Q angle, which most often results
in lateral patellar tilt, lateral subluxation, or lateral dislocation during knee range of
motion. Preoperative risk factors that may increase the risk of patellar maltracking and
instability during the index TKA include femoral and/or tibial malrotation, femoral
trochlear dysplasia, or a previous patellar realignment procedure.7
Several component risk factors also may contribute to patellar maltracking. Femoral or
tibial component internal rotation is detrimental to patellofemoral mechanics. Femoral
component valgus and medialization of the femoral and tibial component change the Q
angle, increasing lateral soft-tissue forces on the patella and causing maltracking.
Femoral component trochlear designs have undergone several generational changes to
improve patellofemoral contact during knee range of motion. Finally, a lateral patellar
button position should be avoided because it may lead to lateral tilt, subluxation, and
medialization of the patient’s native patella.1,4
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The patient often will report pain along the anterior and lateral aspect of the knee.
Knee stiffness, particularly as the knee moves into flexion, is commonly reported.
The patient may report painful catching, clicking, snapping, sensation that the patella will
dislocate, or frank patellar dislocation.
Physical Examination

The physical examination of the knee should begin with inspection, assessing for a joint
effusion.
The patient should be examined in a weight-bearing position to determine overall mechanical
alignment.
Gait examination should assess for an altered or an asymmetric foot-progression angle that
may suggest implant malrotation or a large valgus thrust.
Knee palpation may reveal peripatellar tenderness or a joint effusion.
Ligamentous stability testing
Passive and active knee range of motion may reveal visual patellar subluxation or dislocation.

Patient History/Physical Examination
Patients with patellar maltracking and instability often report anterior and lateral
peripatellar knee pain, particularly with weight-bearing activities and
ascending/descending stairs. Knee stiffness is commonly reported because
patellofemoral mechanics have been altered and soft tissues may be under undue
tension, specifically in knee flexion. Finally, the patient may report painful catching,
clicking, snapping, or reproducible dislocations of the patella.
The physical examination should attempt to identify technical factors that may have
caused aberrancies in the Q angle leading to patellar maltracking. The patient’s knee
should be fully exposed and examined in a weight-bearing position to determine overall
mechanical alignment. Gait examination should include inspection of the foot-
progression angle because an asymmetric in-toeing gait may suggest tibial or femoral
internal rotation. Palpation of the knee often elicits pain along the lateral peripatellar
tissues. Finally, during evaluation of passive and active range of motion, surgeons should
assess for visual evidence of patellar subluxation or dislocation, especially as the knee
progresses into flexion.6
Imaging Studies
Radiography

Radiographs should be carefully reviewed for implant positioning, size, and other causes of
pain or failure of the implants.
The height of the patella (Insall-Salvati ratio) also should be noted.
Three-foot standing radiographs can help determine overall mechanical alignment after TKA.
Patellar views are vital in analyzing patellar thickness, patellar tracking within the femoral
component groove, patellar tilt, and the presence of patellar subluxation or frank dislocation.
Computed Tomography
Metal-suppression CT scans may aid in assessing implant rotation and whether the femoral
and/or tibial component are malrotated.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is rarely indicated to diagnose and manage patellar instability; however, in patients who
sustain an acute fall and report new-onset maltracking after TKA without obvious physical
examination or radiographic findings, MRI may be indicated to ensure an arthrotomy
dehiscence has not occurred.
Differential Diagnosis
Patellofemoral crepitus or crunch syndrome
Patellar clunk syndrome

Differential Diagnosis
Imaging studies may be useful in evaluating a patient in whom patellar maltracking is
suspected. Standing radiographs help determine overall mechanical alignment.
Dedicated knee radiographs allow for assessment of implant positioning and size.
Skyline radiographs provide a static view of the patellofemoral joint and allow for
evaluation for lateral patellar tilt or subluxation, and allow for assessment of the position
of the patellar button. Finally, metal-suppression CT scans may aid in assessment of
implant rotation via fixed anatomic landmarks, such as the transepicondylar axis and the

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management may be indicated if the symptoms are tolerable and do not
compromise the patient’s daily function.
Nonsurgical treatment also may be considered in patients who are medically unfit to undergo
additional surgical treatment.
Nonsurgical management includes physical therapy to focus on quadriceps strengthening,
especially the vastus medialis, to attempt to centralize the patella; a patellar sleeve or brace
and/or taping also can be used.
Surgical Management
In patients with an acute injury and isolated arthrotomy dehiscence, primary repair of the
arthrotomy with the use of heavy nonabsorbable sutures is indicated.
In patients with symptomatic mild patellar maltracking and well-positioned components, a
soft-tissue procedure, including lateral release and vastus medialis imbrication, can be
performed; however, this rarely is indicated.
Most often, resolution of patellar maltracking includes revision of the femoral, tibial, and/or
patellar component, with or without soft-tissue procedures.
Revision surgery to correct patellar instability after TKA is based on preoperative clinical
assessment, imaging studies, and intraoperative findings.
Indications
Clinical evidence of patellar instability (patient history, physical examination, imaging studies),
postoperative pain, and dysfunction leading to compromised quality of life
Failed nonsurgical management

Techniques/Procedures
Before making an incision, ligamentous balancing and patellofemoral tracking should be
assessed under an anesthetic to note the technical modifications that need to be made during
revision surgery.
The revision procedure is performed via a standard medial parapatellar approach.
Surgeons should maintain a low threshold to perform an extensile procedure, such as the
quadriceps snip, to subluxate the extensor mechanism and improve implant exposure.
Carefully assess current implant rotation and positioning before implant removal:
Femoral component
The transepicondylar axis can be drawn or marked for reference.
Mark the current femoral rotation to ensure the revised component will be externally
rotated relative to the component.
Tibial component
A useful technique is to attach an insertion handle with the polyethylene removed to the
tibial baseplate and observe the rotation of the tibia relative to the tibial tubercle from a
bird’s-eye-view position.
Patellar component
A central or laterally positioned patellar component should be revised to a superomedial
position to reduce the risk of patellar instability.
Implants requiring revision are removed at the implant-cement interface via standard
techniques.
Tibial component revision
Tibial component revision requires careful assessment of rotation; the target usually is the
middle third of the tibial tubercle.
The tibial component should not be medialized, and adequate bony support for the
baseplate should be ensured.
Any varus-valgus malalignment should be corrected.
Femoral component revision
In revising the distal femoral cuts, placement of the component in excessive valgus
malalignment should be avoided.

Excessive femoral component flexion may lead to patellofemoral impingement and
maltracking and should be corrected.
The femoral component should be placed laterally but should not result in excessive
overhang and impingement on lateral soft tissues.
Femoral rotation is critical; after the tibia is prepared, the flexion space should be
rectangular, which may aid in setting femoral rotation.
Care should be taken to address posterolateral bone loss because this tends to lead to
femoral component internal rotation; a low threshold should exist to augment the
posterolateral femur with the use of modular metal augments.
Patellar component revision
To optimize patellofemoral tracking, the patellar component should be placed medially.
Patellofemoral overstuffing also should be corrected because it may lead to lateral patellar
tilt and subluxation during knee flexion.
The patellar component should track centrally and, ideally, contact the medial femoral condyle
through range of motion via a no fingers surgical technique.
If the patella continues to track laterally or subluxate and no rotatory or angular deformities
present, then a soft-tissue procedure may be indicated.
Lateral release
This involves release of the lateral retinaculum and the lateral patellofemoral ligament.
The procedure can be performed via an outside-in or inside-out technique; with either
technique, the synovium should not be compromised.
Identify and protect the superolateral genicular arterial branch to the patella to limit the risk
of patellar osteonecrosis.
Vastus medialis imbrication
The vastus medialis should be mobilized proximally up the thigh.
Via a pants-over-vest suture technique, the vastus medialis can be imbricated over the
superolateral patella and the vastus medialis to increase the tension of the medial soft-tissue
envelope.

Techniques/Procedures
Most revision procedures for the management of patellar maltracking and instability
should be performed via a medial parapatellar approach to allow for extensile exposure
techniques if necessary. Because both components often are revised, a quadriceps snip

removal. Two stay sutures at the proximal extent of snip are useful for guiding repair of
the snip at the end of the procedure because the extensor mechanism must be
anatomically reapproximated to ensure optimal patellofemoral tracking.
Before removal, assessment and marking of the current implant rotation is useful so
appropriate changes can be made to improve patellar tracking. Femoral rotation can be
guided by the transepicondylar axis. A tibial baseplate insertion handle or straight
instrument can be used to judge tibial rotation. By looking down from a bird’s-eye view,
the surgeon can assess baseplate rotation relative to the tibial tubercle. The patella can
be carefully everted with the knee in full extension to assess implant positioning. If the
patellar button is central or lateral, it should be revised to a superomedial position to
optimize patellar tracking.
After the implants have been removed via standard techniques, reconstruction begins
with the tibial component. In most patients, the revised tibial cut will be made via
intramedullary referencing. A drop-rod may be a useful augment to confirm alignment of
the resection and to ensure the cut is made with the jig centered over the medial third of
the tibial tubercle. The baseplate trial also should be rotated such that it transects the
medial third of the tibial tubercle. The surgeon also should avoid medializing the tibial
component because this may change the Q angle and affect patellar tracking.
Posterolateral overhang of the tibial baseplate is not uncommon if correct implant
rotation is set.
On the femoral side, the revised cuts often are based on intramedullary referencing.
Corrections that should be made to avoid patellar instability include excessive femoral
valgus, which increases the Q angle, and femoral component flexion, which may lead to
patellofemoral impingement and maltracking. Femoral component rotation is assessed
relative to the previous implant position and the transepicondylar axis, and the flexion
space should be rectangular with the knee in 90° of flexion. A pitfall of femoral
component revisions is not addressing posterolateral bone loss. If this bone is not
reconstructed, usually with the use of metal femoral augments, the femoral component
will be inserted with internal rotation. The surgeon should maintain a low threshold to
augment the posterolateral femur in revision procedures for the management of

Finally, the patellar button should be revised to a medial position to improve patellar
tracking. The surgeon also should avoid overstuffing the patellofemoral joint because
this may lead to lateral patellar tilt and subluxation of the patella during knee flexion.
After the trial implants have been inserted, patellofemoral tracking through a full range
of motion should be assessed. The tourniquet should be turned down at this point
because excessive tension on the quadriceps may artificially influence poor patellar
tracking. The patellar component should track centrally and contact the medial femoral
condyle through range of motion. A single suture or a towel clip can be used to
reapproximate the medial flap of the arthrotomy to better reproduce soft-tissue tension
during tracking. If the patella tracks laterally or subluxates and the surgeon verifies that
implant rotation and alignment has been optimized, then a soft-tissue procedure will
improve tracking.
The most common soft-tissue procedure includes a lateral release. With the knee in
extension, soft-tissue retractors are used to expose the lateral border of the patella.
Under direct visualization, the lateral retinaculum and the lateral patellofemoral
ligament are released, beginning at the inferior pole of the patella and working
proximally approximately 1 to 2 cm lateral to the lateral border of the patella. The
release depth should not compromise the synovium. If additional release is required
proximally, the surgeon should identify and protect the superolateral genicular artery to
the patella to limit the risk of patellar osteonecrosis.4 A lateral release can be combined
with an imbrication of the vastus medialis to realign the extensor mechanism more
medially in the femoral groove.

Outcomes

Outcomes
Most studies examining the effect of revision TKA for the management of patellofemoral
maltracking are limited to case series. The most commonly reported technical errors that
lead to patellofemoral maltracking include implant malrotation and imbalance of the soft
tissues, specifically the lateral retinaculum. Patients who have undergone revision
procedures have improved patient-reported outcome scores; however, many patients
still report pain and dysfunction after the procedure.9,10
Patellar Clunk
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Patellar clunk is a syndrome that occurs after TKA that is characterized by a noticeable
displacement of the patella, or clunking, as the knee is moved from flexion to extension.11
This displacement results in crepitus and pain with range of motion.
Epidemiology
The exact incidence of patellar clunk after TKA is unknown; however, the reported incidence
ranges from 3.9% to 13.5%.12-14
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Patellar clunk occurs after TKA if fibrous tissue or hyperplastic synovium forms at the superior
pole of the patella and the junction of the quadriceps tendon.15
The syndrome occurs almost exclusively in posterior-stabilized TKA implant designs.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Patellar clunk is a commonly cited syndrome that occurs after TKA, almost exclusively
with posterior-stabilized implant designs. The exact incidence of patellar clunk is
unknown; however, studies have reported that the incidence ranges from 3.9% to
13.5%.12-14 As the patient’s knee moves from extension to flexion, fibrous tissue
proximal to the superior pole of the patella engages the intercondylar box of the femoral
component, causing patellar displacement, or a clunking sensation through range of
motion.15
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The exact etiology leading to the fibrous tissue that may cause patellar clunk is unknown.
Plausible causes may include iatrogenic injury to the quadriceps tendon proximal to the
superior pole of the patella during TKA or repetitive microtrauma from impingement of the
quadriceps tendon on the femoral component.15

Valgus gonarthrosis
Previous knee surgery
Presence of synovial hyperplasia/fibrosis around quadriceps tendon
Component Risk Factors
Posterior-stabilized design
High intercondylar box ratio
Undersized patellar component

Risk Factors
The exact etiology of patellar clunk syndrome after TKA is unknown. Some plausible
explanations may include iatrogenic trauma to the quadriceps tendon just proximal to
the superior pole of the patella during the reconstruction. In addition, recurring
impingement of the quadriceps tendon on the femoral component during range of
motion may lead to formation of a fibrous nodule over time. Preoperative risk factors for
patellar clunk include patella baja, valgus gonarthrosis, previous knee surgery, and the
presence of fibrosis or synovial hyperplasia around the quadriceps tendon.
Certain component characteristics and reconstructive changes have been identified as
risk factors in the literature. Patellar clunk occurs exclusively with posterior-stabilized
knee designs. The incidence also is higher in femoral prostheses in which the
intercondylar box ratio is elevated.1,15 This ratio is the distance from the posterior
extent of the femoral component to the top of the box divided by the entire
anteroposterior dimension of the prosthesis. Other reported risk factors include an
undersized patellar component, inferior patellar component placement, flexion of the
femoral implant, and anterior tibial tray placement.16
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patellar clunking often occurs 3 to 12 months postoperatively.
The patient will report a pop, catch, or clunk with daily activities.
Anterior knee pain is commonly associated with patellar clunk.
The patient may report activity-related swelling or a recurring joint effusion.

The patient should be examined in a weight-bearing position to determine overall mechanical

Active and passive range of motion of the knee should be examined.
Typically, the patella will clunk from flexion to approximately 30° to 45° of extension.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs should be carefully reviewed for implant positioning, size, and other causes of
pain or failure of the implants.
Review of preoperative radiographs may be useful to discern any risk factors that may have
predicted patellar clunk.
Ultrasonography
May be useful to identify fibrous tissue accumulation in the suprapatellar region or the distal
insertion of the quadriceps onto the superior patellar pole
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Rarely indicated but typically will show scar formation posterior to the quadriceps tendon at
the level of the superior patellar pole
Differential Diagnosis
Patellofemoral crepitus or crunch syndrome
Patellofemoral maltracking/subluxation

Evaluation/Diagnosis
The diagnosis of patellar clunk syndrome should begin with a complete patient history.
The syndrome typically occurs approximately 3 to 9 months postoperatively, which may
coincide with the formation of the fibrous nodule as the soft tissue is remodeling

knee moves from flexion to extension. This often results in anterior knee pain and
recurring knee effusions with daily activities.
On physical examination, the knee should be fully exposed with the patient fully bearing
weight. Assessment of overall mechanical alignment is important because it may
influence patellar tracking. The gait cycle should be examined to determine if an internal
foot-progression angle exists that may affect patellofemoral mechanics. Knee range of
motion assessment will elicit a clunk as the knee progresses from flexion to
approximately 30° to 45° short of full extension.
Although patellar clunk syndrome is a clinical diagnosis, radiographs of the affected knee
may be useful to determine if any of the component or technical risk factors that may
predispose the patient to patellar clunk are present. Review of radiographs also may
ensure that other causes of mechanical failure are considered, such as loosening of the
patellar component. In combination with radiographs, the operating room report or
implant stickers may help identify the type of implants used during the index procedure
because some posterior-stabilized designs are associated with higher reported
incidences of patellar clunk. Finally, ultrasonography may be a useful adjunct to identify
fibrous tissue along the superior pole of the patella or the distal insertion of the
quadriceps tendon (Figure 1).

strain on the patellofemoral joint and may result in late failure of the extensor
mechanism.1,11,14-16 Finally, during complex revision TKA with the use of

Primary Repair With Augmentation
Because of the high failure rate of primary repair alone, augmentation with the use of
allograft, synthetic mesh, and/or autograft tissue (ie, hamstring tendons) has been
described.30,32-34
Indications
Acute to subacute extensor mechanism disruption (patellar tendon, quadriceps tendon,
patellar fracture) with adequate viable soft tissue for primary repair
Contraindications
Active periprosthetic joint infection
Noncompliance with prolonged immobilization and prolonged rehabilitation
Techniques/procedures
Allograft tendon augmentation and synthetic mesh augmentation include techniques similar
to those already described with only subtle modifications, depending on if the disruption is
at the level of the quadriceps, patella, or patellar tendon.
Hamstring autograft techniques have been described in case reports without a consensus on
the specific surgical technical steps.33,34
